newsitem.title: CHINA: Clarke says sees more UK listings for China firms.
newsitem.headline: Clarke says sees more UK listings for China firms.

text.p: Most Chinese companies that tap world capital markets will turn to Hong Kong but a significant number will list shares in London, British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Tuesday.

Speaking after meetings with Chinese financial officials, Clarke also said he believed Beijing would license the first British insurance firm to do business on the domestic market in the not too distant future.
"I am quite happy to accept that most Chinese listings will be in Hong Kong," he told reporters.
"But I think there will be a significant number in London as well."
Hong Kong has captured the lion's share of foreign listings by Chinese companies, although New York and Singapore have made inroads as well.
China and Britain signed a memorandum of understanding in October last year, paving the way for capital-hungry Chinese companies to list shares on the London stock exchange.
Electric power firm Datang Power Generation is expected to become the first Chinese company to offer shares in London soon. It plans a dual listing in London and Hong Kong.
"We expect more companies to follow," Clarke said.
He also expressed optimism that a British insurance firm would gain access to the fast-growing Chinese market, although he declined to be specific about a timetable or name the firm.
China has been gradually opening its insurance market to foreign companies but only a few -- none of them British -- have been permitted to write policies in China so far.
This has led to speculation that Sino-British friction over political reforms in Hong Kong was to blame.

China and Britain have been at loggerheads over Beijing's plans to dismantle Hong Kong's elected legislature and replace it with an appointed body after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.
Clarke said he hoped political considerations were not distorting financial decisions.

Clarke, who met Vice-Premier Li Lanqing, Finance Minister Liu Zhongli and top securities regulator Zhou Daojiong during his brief stay, said China and Britain would step up financial cooperation with a programme to bring Beijing's financial regulators to London for training.
